text: Diabetes has become extremely widespread among us. In almost every Egyptian household, you may find one or two people living with diabetes.
In my view, we have misunderstood the disease, treated it incorrectly, and continued along a treatment path that also handled its complications incorrectly.
Eventually, serious complications can develop, including problems in the legs and, in severe cases, amputations of the extremities.
I believe one major issue in diabetes is fatty liver, while treatment often focuses mainly on the pancreas.
What happens with the liver? Each time you eat, levels of fat and glucose in the blood rise.
The liver works to process and regulate these increases. In my view, repeated spikes become more problematic when fatty liver is present.
Then, each time glucose rises after eating, repeated spikes can also drive insulin levels higher.
According to this explanation, insulin resistance develops, and the pancreas eventually struggles to cope with repeatedly elevated glucose.
I believe treatment often focuses on pancreatic failure, while the underlying problem is fatty liver and the dietary habits contributing to it.
By changing those eating habits, I believe fatty liver can improve, blood sugar can improve, and medication needs may sometimes decrease.
Even if diabetes is a chronic condition, the goal should be to control it well and, under medical supervision, reduce medication when appropriate.
If every follow-up visit only results in another medication being added, that does not necessarily mean the diabetes itself is improving.
The aim, in my view, is to address the underlying problem and keep blood sugar under control rather than simply following the disease as it progresses.
That is why I say the long-term solution begins with the dietary system.
